claim: Mice leaving from a stable entrance learned to efficiently navigate to hidden food without the need for landmarks.
source: Mice leaving from a stable entrance learned to efficiently navigate to the food without the need for landmarks.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from static entrance experiments showing trajectory optimization and hole check patterns.

claim: The computed 'target estimation vector' (TEV) closely approximated the mice's route and hole check distribution after learning.
source: After learning, the computed 'target estimation vector' (TEV) closely approximated the mice's route and its hole check distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory and hole check analyses presented in Figures 4, 5, 7, and 8, showing alignment between TEV and actual mouse behavior.

claim: The TEV required learning both the direction and distance of the start to food vector.
source: The TEV required learning both the direction and distance of the start to food vector, and our data suggests that different learning dynamics underlie these estimates.
evidence: This is supported by data showing different learning kinetics for direction (learned by trial 6) versus distance (approaching optimal by trial 14), as shown in Figures 3F and 4I.

claim: After learning the location of two food sites, mice took a shortcut between the sites.
source: Finally, we provide the first demonstration that, after learning the location of two food sites, the mice took a shortcut between the sites, demonstrating that they had generated a cognitive map.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data from the two-food-location experiment showing mice navigating directly from Site B to Site A without prior reinforcement of this route (Figures 6, 7).

claim: Mice can use localized odor sources as landmarks for spatial learning.
source: Mice can use odors as landmarks for spatial learning (Fischler-Ruiz et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A 'spatial map' can be generated by self-motion cues anchored to stable landmarks.
source: Research on the interaction of landmark and self-motion cues has concluded that a 'spatial map' can be generated by self-motion cues anchored to stable landmarks (McNaughton et al., 1996; Burgess, 2006; Chen et al., 2013; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Mice did not use landmarks but required only minimal cues (stable start location, self-motion signals, and active sensing) to learn to find food.
source: We found that mice did not use the landmarks but required only minimal cues, namely a stable start location, self-motion signals and active sensing (hole checks), to learn to find food.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from random entrance experiments (where landmarks were present but mice failed to learn), static entrance experiments (successful learning), rotation experiments (mice went to REL not actual target), and control experiments without landmarks or in darkness.

claim: When mice were transferred to another start site after learning, their TEVs rotated and pointed to the rotationally equivalent location (REL) instead of the target.
source: When, after learning, the mice were transferred to another start site, their TEVs also rotated and then pointed to the 'rotationally equivalent location' (REL) instead of the target, therefore demonstrating that they were utilizing self-motion cues for navigation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data from rotation probe trials shown in Figure 5, where mice navigated to REL locations after their start position was rotated.

claim: This is the first demonstration that a stable start location and self-motion cues are sufficient for a rodent to compute a cognitive map.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a stable start location and self-motion cues are sufficient for a rodent to compute a cognitive map.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and their experimental findings showing shortcut behavior without landmarks.

claim: The Hidden Food Maze (HFM) arena is 120 cm in diameter with walls 45 cm tall.
source: The floor of the arena is 120 cm in diameter, and the walls are 45 cm tall.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental apparatus shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The maze floor has 100 holes randomly dispersed throughout the surface.
source: The circular floor is 120 cm in diameter and has 100 holes (1.2 cm diameter) randomly dispersed throughout the surface, with 25 holes in each quadrant.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus design.

claim: The pattern of holes is rotationally symmetrical so it looks the same when rotated 90°, 180°, or 270°.
source: The pattern of the holes is rotationally symmetrical, so the pattern looks the same regardless of whether the floor is rotated 90°, 180°, or 270° with respect to the mouse's entrance.
evidence: This is a design feature of the experimental apparatus intended to eliminate geometric cues.

claim: Mice initially explored the maze by following the wall (thigmotaxis) before exploring the maze center.
source: In agreement with previous work (Fonio et al., 2009), we observed that mice initially explored the maze by following the wall (thigmotaxis) on round trips of increasing complexity before they explored the maze center.
evidence: This observation is supported by pretraining trajectory data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with cited prior work.

claim: In random entrance experiments, mice showed persistent complex search trajectories throughout the learning period.
source: The food-restricted mice showed persistent complex search trajectories throughout the learning period (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by trajectory examples in Figure 2A and B showing irregular trajectories in both early and late learning trials.

claim: In random entrance experiments, latency to reach the food target was significantly negatively correlated with trial number.
source: The latency to reach the food target was significantly negatively correlated with trial number (statistics in Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D (R=-0.61; p=0.008; N=8).

claim: In random entrance experiments, there was no significant difference in latency between the first and last trials.
source: but with a non-significant difference between the first and last trials (N=8; First trial mean ± SD = 151.34±148.91 s; Last trial mean ± SD = 80.38±43.86 s; p=0.2602).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the random entrance experiment data.

claim: In random entrance experiments, mice spent similar time in each quadrant during the probe trial.
source: mice did not appear to exhibit spatial search strategies (Figure 2C) given that the time spent in each quadrant during the probe trial is similar (target quadrant = 28.78%, other quadrants = 24.93%, 28.04%, 18.25%; one-way ANOVA: p=0.070574, F-ratio=2.71621
evidence: This is supported by probe trial data shown in Figure 2C and statistical analysis.

claim: In random entrance experiments, speed was significantly positively correlated with trial number.
source: We found a corresponding significant positive correlation of speed and trial number (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2E showing R=0.7; p=0.002.

claim: In random entrance experiments, there was no significant correlation between normalized trajectory length and trial number.
source: There is no significant correlation of this quantity and trial number (p=0.295).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of normalized trajectory length data in random entrance experiments.

claim: In random entrance experiments, hole checking density remained constant between the first and second halves of any trial.
source: However, the hole checking density (ratio between number of checks and distance travelled) remains constant between the first and second halves of any trial (Figure 2G), suggesting mice did not anticipate where the food is placed.
evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 2G indicating no change in hole check density across trial halves.

claim: In static entrance experiments, mice greatly improved their trajectory efficiency after training.
source: Mice greatly improved their trajectory efficiency after training (Figure 3A and B), with distance and latency to food plateauing around trial 7.
evidence: This is demonstrated by trajectory examples in Figure 3A and B and quantitative data in Figures 3D-F.

claim: In static entrance experiments, during the probe trial mice spent the most time searching in the target quadrant (44.26%).
source: During the probe trial, mice spent the most time searching in the target quadrant (44.26%; Figure 3C), compared to the time spent in the other quadrants, respectively 19.38% (p=0.007), 16.55% (p=0.0065), 19.81% (p=0.007; p-values obtained for a pairwise t-test and adjusted for multiple comparisons via the Benjamini-Hochberg method).
evidence: This is supported by probe trial heatmap data in Figure 3C and statistical analysis.

claim: In static entrance experiments, latency to target strongly decreased over trials.
source: The latency to target strongly decreased over trials (Figure 3D) and the last trial latency was significantly reduced compared to the first (N=8; First trial mean ± SD = 255.39±153.28 s; Last trial mean ± SD = 7.38±4.03 s; p=0.004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3D showing strong negative correlation (R=-0.96; p<10^-7).

claim: In static entrance experiments, speed dramatically increased over trials.
source: The speed dramatically increased over trials (Figure 3E) and the ending speed was significantly greater than the initial speed (N=8, First trial mean ± SD = 6.04±2.48 cm/s; Last trial mean ± SD = 17.25±4.64 cm/s; p=0.0002).
evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 3E with R=0.9; p=0.0001.

claim: In static entrance experiments, normalized trajectory length strongly negatively correlated with trial number and became almost optimal.
source: The normalized trajectory length strongly negatively correlated with trial number (Figure 3F) and the final normalized length greatly reduced (N=8; First trial mean ± SD = 18.02±11.36; Last trial mean ± SD = 1.40±0.50; p=0.0061), becoming almost optimal (Rosenberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3F showing R=-0.96; p<10^-7.

claim: In static entrance experiments, it takes a minimum of K=6 trials for learning the distance to the target.
source: Now the fitting of the function dtotal = B exp(-Trial/K) yielded K=5.6 ± 0.5 with a CV = 0.08; the mean is therefore a reliable estimate of total distance travelled. We interpret this to indicate that it takes a minimum number of K=6 trials for learning the distance to the target
evidence: This is based on exponential fitting of distance data from static entrance experiments.

claim: In static entrance experiments, hole checking density significantly decreased with trial number in the first half of trajectories.
source: The density significantly decreased with trial number in the first half of trajectories (R=−0.54; p=0.0455, Figure 3G) but not the second half (R=0.17; p=0.559, Figure 3G).
evidence: This is shown by statistical analysis of hole check density data in Figure 3G.

claim: In static entrance experiments, hole checks happened significantly closer to the target in the second half of the trajectory.
source: The hole checks also happened significantly closer to the target in the second half of the trajectory (Figure 3H; First trial mean ± SD = 48.06±11.50 cm; Last trial mean ± SD = 3.13±5.70 cm; p=3 × 10–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3H showing decreasing distance of hole checks to food over trials.

claim: In static entrance experiments, the probability of checking holes increases as the mouse approaches the food after learning.
source: A remarkable effect of learning is that the probability of checking holes increases as the mouse approaches the food (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is shown by probability density distributions in Figure 3I comparing trial 1 and trial 14.

claim: In static entrance training, the deviation between TEV and target vector was rapidly reduced to 5.16° ± 0.20° by trial 6.
source: While the random entrance mice had a persistent deviation between TEV and target of more than 70o, the static entrance mice were able to learn the direction of the target almost perfectly by trial 6 (TEV-target deviation in first trial mean ± SD = 57.27o ± 41.61o; last trial mean ± SD = 5.16o ± 0.20o; p=0.0166).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEV-target deviation data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Static entrance mice had significantly higher density of hole checks near the target compared to far from the target.
source: However, static entrance mice had significantly higher density of hole checks near the target (Figure 4K; p-values: random-far vs. static-far=0.005; static-far vs. random-near=0.03; random-near vs. static-near=0.01).
evidence: This is shown by statistical comparison of hole check density data in Figure 4K.

claim: Following all rotations, mice searched at the REL instead of the correct location for the food reward.
source: Following all rotations, mice searched at the REL instead of the correct location for the food reward regardless of the arena having wall cues (Figure 5A, B and C), meaning that they were not using landmarks to compensate for rotation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by trajectory data from rotation experiments shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: The trajectory kinetics of the 180°-rotated probe for reaching the REL target is indistinguishable from the kinetics of the last trial of static entrance for reaching the true target.
source: In fact, the trajectory kinetics of the 180o-rotated probe for reaching the REL target (mean ± SD latency = 4.80 ± 3.06 s; speed = 14.60 ± 5.21 cm/s; normalized distance to REL = 1.96 ± 0.90) is indistinguishable (within one SD or less) from the kinetics of the last trial of static entrance for reaching the true target.
evidence: This is based on comparison of kinetic parameters between rotated probe trials and final training trials.

claim: The learning curve of mice with or without 2D wall cues were not significantly different.
source: The learning curve of mice with or without the 2D wall cues were not significantly different (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by control experiment data in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A comparing training with and without visual cues.

claim: Mice that were well trained in the lighted maze still showed the same learning curve when tested in complete darkness.
source: Mice that were well trained in the lighted maze were given trials in complete darkness. These mice still showed the same learning curve compared to untrained mice or mice following rotation (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiment data in Figure 4—figure supplement 5C-D.

claim: Mice trained and tested in total darkness were able to learn the food location in the absence of visual and olfactory cues.
source: The mice were still able to learn the food location in the absence of visual and olfactory cues (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by control experiment data in Figure 4—figure supplement 5E-F comparing mice trained in darkness versus light.

claim: During the learning of target A, the distance of the mouse to the future location of target B was always larger than that expected by chance.
source: During the learning of target A, the distance of the mouse to the future location of target B was always larger than that expected by chance, that is to a randomly chosen location in the maze (see Materials and methods, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A showing mice kept farther from future target B location than expected by chance.

claim: Five of eight mice went from B to A via varying trajectories in the Probe B-A trial.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6D and the Shortcut video (Video 1) (all mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2), five of eight mice were observed to go from B to A via varying trajectories (namely, mice numbered 33, 35, 36, 57, and 59).
evidence: This is documented by trajectory data shown in Figure 6D, Video 1, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Two mice went first to A and subsequently to B via direct or indirect routes in the Probe B-A trial.
source: Two (number 58 and 60) of the remaining three mice went first to A and subsequently to B via direct or indirect routes; these mice had previously taken direct routes to B, suggesting that going to A first is not due to a learning deficiency.
evidence: This is based on analysis of individual mouse trajectories in the Probe B-A trial.

claim: All Probe B-A values are significantly different from trial 1-B and from randomized B-A trajectories.
source: Conversely, all the Probe B-A values are significantly different both from trial 1-B and from randomized B-A trajectories (see Materials and methods; p<0.05; except for the density of hole checks which is statistically equal for all considered trials, Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical comparisons shown in Figures 6E-H.

claim: In the rotated probe B-A, mice went to the REL of B and then to the REL of A.
source: In the rotated probe B-A, the mice went to the REL of B and then to the REL of A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by trajectory and hole check data from the rotated two-food-location experiment shown in Figure 8.

claim: The displacement map and hole check spatial distribution in rotated probe B-A pointed from REL B to REL A instead of B to A.
source: The displacement map, hole check spatial distribution and TEV now all pointed from REL B to REL A (instead of B to A).
evidence: This is shown by displacement and hole check maps in Figure 8G and H.

claim: Target direction is likely estimated from the activity of head direction cells.
source: As noted below, the food direction is likely estimated from the activity of head direction cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid and precise learning of target direction and the known properties of head direction cells in the literature.

claim: The neural mechanisms by which distance from start to food is estimated are not known.
source: The neural mechanisms by which distance from start to food is estimated are not known (but see Engelmann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Path integration uses self-motion signals to update the animal's estimated location on its internal cognitive map.
source: Path integration uses self-motion signals to update the animal's estimated location on its internal cognitive map.
evidence: This is a statement of established understanding in the field of spatial navigation.

claim: Path integration gain has been shown to be plastic and regulated by landmarks.
source: Path integration gain has been shown to be plastic and regulated by landmarks (Jayakumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Path integration gain can be directly recalibrated by self-motion signals, albeit not as effectively as by landmarks.
source: a recent study has revealed that path integration gain can also be directly recalibrated by self-motion signals (Madhav et al., 2024), albeit not as effectively as by landmarks (Jayakumar et al., 2019; Madhav et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: External cues can control hippocampal neuron place fields.
source: Extensive research has shown that external cues can control hippocampal neuron place fields (Chen et al., 2013; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011; Muller and Kubie, 1987)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: External cues can control the gain of the path integrator.
source: Extensive research has shown that external cues can control hippocampal neuron place fields (Chen et al., 2013; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011; Muller and Kubie, 1987) and the gain of the path integrator (Jayakumar et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The hippocampus and closely connected cortical areas generate a cognitive map.
source: It is further proposed that the hippocampus and closely connected cortical areas generate a cognitive map (McNaughton et al., 2006; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is a statement of a major hypothesis in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Rodent vision is important for tasks such as navigating complex environments, finding shelter, prey capture and predator avoidance.
source: Rodent vision is important for tasks such as navigating complex environments, finding shelter, prey capture and predator avoidance (see Saleem and Busse, 2023 for a review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Previous behavioral and physiological studies suggested that the wall cues used could be resolved by the mouse visual system.
source: Previous behavioral and physiological studies suggested that our wall cues could be resolved by the mouse visual system (Jacobs et al., 2009; Long et al., 2015; Prusky and Douglas, 2004; Prusky et al., 2000; Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on mouse vision.

claim: Rats have been shown to be able to solve the random start task in the Morris Water Maze.
source: Rats have been shown to be able to solve this task in the Morris Water Maze (MWM; Morris, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the classic Morris Water Maze study.

claim: Previous studies showed that mice can use distal cues for spatial learning under different experimental conditions.
source: Previous studies showed that mice can use distal cues for spatial learning under different experimental conditions, such as in a one-dimensional T-maze, linear track, or when there are multiple highly salient cues (Morris, 1981; Chapillon and Roullet, 1996; Hébert et al., 2017; Rogers et al., 2017; Youngstrom and Strowbridge, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on mouse spatial learning.

claim: Behavioral experiments showed the importance of landmark stability for spatial learning.
source: This view is supported by behavioral experiments that showed the importance of landmark stability for spatial learning (Biegler and Morris, 1996; Biegler and Morris, 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral research.

claim: Place cells are not controlled by 'unreliable landmarks'.
source: and that place cells are not controlled by 'unreliable landmarks' (Jeffery, 1998; Knierim et al., 1995; Save et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological research.

claim: Many place cell responses observed in the presence of visual cues will remain after these cues are removed in rats.
source: Two studies suggest that, in the rat, CA1 place fields will remain stable in the absence of visual cues. Many place cells responses observed in the presence of visual cues will remain after these cues are removed; the authors conclude that self-motion cues are sufficient to maintain normal place fields (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on rat place cells.

claim: Vision is not necessary for the development of normal firing of hippocampal place cells in blind rats.
source: Experiments with blind rats have shown vision is not necessary for the development of normal firing of hippocampal place cells (Save et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on blind rats.

claim: Distal visual cues and self-motion cues may be required to activate place cells representing allocentric space.
source: Analyses of spatial learning in VR versus RW (rats) suggested that distal visual cues, and self-motion (i.e. proprioceptive, vestibular) cues may be required to activate place cells representing allocentric space.
evidence: This is based on inference from cited studies comparing virtual reality and real world navigation.

claim: In the absence of distal visual cues, CA1 cells preferentially encoded distance traveled during learned trajectories toward a food goal.
source: In the absence of distal visual cues, CA1 cells preferentially encoded distance traveled during learned trajectories toward a food goal (Aghajan et al., 2015; Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological research.

claim: Rats can learn to navigate in VR from different start locations to a hidden goal using very salient distal visual cues.
source: Rats can learn to navigate, in VR, from different start locations to a hidden goal using very salient distal visual cues (Moore et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Unlike RW spatial learning, CA1 pyramidal cells in VR only weakly encoded allocentric spatial information but instead primarily encoded trajectory distance and head direction.
source: Unlike RW spatial learning, CA1 pyramidal cells then only weakly encoded allocentric spatial information (place fields) but instead, primarily encoded trajectory distance and head direction – thus, these cells may comprise a possible neural implementation of the behavioral TEV.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to prior research and inference about neural implementation of TEV.

claim: A subset of hippocampal (CA1) neurons in the bat were reported to encode the direction and/or distance of a hidden goal.
source: A subset of hippocampal (CA1) neurons in the bat were reported to encode the direction and/or distance of a hidden goal (Sarel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on bat hippocampal neurons.

claim: CA1 convergence sink (ConSink) place cells are directional place cells that can encode local direction towards a goal.
source: Recently described CA1 convergence sink (ConSink) place cells (Ormond and O'Keefe, 2022) may also have the properties needed to account for the learned start-to-food trajectories we observed. ConSink cells are directional place cells that can encode local direction towards a goal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research on ConSink cells.

claim: ConSink cells will, with training, shift their direction tuning to a new goal.
source: ConSink cells will, with training, shift their direction tuning to a new goal.
evidence: This is a property of ConSink cells described in cited research.

claim: The ConSink population vector average points directly from start to goal.
source: The ConSink population vector average, like the TEV, then points directly from start to goal.
evidence: This is a property of ConSink cells described in cited research, compared to the behavioral TEV.

claim: ConSink-like cells were reported in the CA1 of a mouse foraging in an open field, but their direction tuning was not pointed towards a singular goal.
source: ConSink-like cells were reported in the CA1 of a mouse foraging in an open field, but their direction tuning was not pointed towards a singular goal (Jercog et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Numerous studies have reported that goal sites are overrepresented by CA1 place cells.
source: Numerous studies have reported that goal sites are overrepresented by CA1 place cells (Nyberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review or research paper.

claim: The requirements for goal overrepresentation are stereotyped trajectories directed towards an invisible memory-based goal associated with reward.
source: The requirements for such overrepresentation are that there are stereotyped trajectories directed towards an invisible memory-based goal associated with reward (Nyberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Goal-related place cells are activated before the goal is reached.
source: Interestingly, the 'goal-related place cells' are activated before the goal is reached (Nyberg et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Behavioral time scale plasticity (BTSP) has been proposed to be the cellular mechanism that generates new CA1 place fields at important locations, including those associated with reward.
source: Behavioral time scale plasticity (BTSP) has been proposed to be the cellular mechanism that generates new CA1 place fields at important locations, including those associated with reward (Bittner et al., 2015; Bittner et al., 2017; Milstein et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on BTSP.

claim: BTSP operates up to a ~3 s time frame.
source: BTSP operates up to a ~3 s time frame.
evidence: This is a property of BTSP described in cited research.

claim: BTSP is bidirectional and can result in CA1 place fields translocating with experience.
source: BTSP is bidirectional and can result in CA1 place fields translocating with experience (Milstein et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Active sensing is critical for electric fish spatial learning.
source: Active sensing is critical for electric fish spatial learning (Engelmann et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on electric fish.

claim: Active sensing is known to potentiate or induce CA1 cell place fields.
source: and is also known to potentiate or induce CA1 cell place fields (Monaco et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: With spatial learning in static entrance, temporally 'close to target' hole checks increase relative to temporally distant hole checks and converge to the target site.
source: With spatial learning (static entrance), temporally 'close to target' hole checks increase relative to temporally distant hole checks and converge to the target site.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing evolution of hole checks within 3s of finding food.

claim: The O'Keefe and Nadel text connected hippocampal place cells to the abstract concept of a cognitive map developed by Tolman.
source: The O'Keefe and Nadel text (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978) connected hippocampal place cells to the abstract concept of a cognitive map developed by Tolman, 1948, and this linkage has been generally supported with few dissenting views (Bennett, 1996; Grieves and Dudchenko, 2013; Benhamou, 1996; Shamash et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the history and current state of the field, supported by citations.

claim: The criteria for a cognitive map are animals taking unrehearsed shortcuts, detours or novel routes.
source: The criteria for a cognitive map are of animals taking unrehearsed shortcuts (Tolman et al., 1946b), detours (Tolman, 1948) or novel routes (Morris, 1981).
evidence: This is a statement of established criteria in the field, supported by citations to classic papers.

claim: Unrehearsed shortcut behavior using only self-motion cues and a fixed start location has only been shown in humans prior to this study.
source: To the best of our knowledge, unrehearsed shortcut behavior using only self-motion cues and a fixed start location has only been shown in humans (Etienne and Jeffery, 2004; Landau et al., 1984).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Head direction tuning may be impaired in sighted mice navigating in darkness.
source: A recent study has shown that placing sighted mice in darkness impairs entorhinal cortex head direction cell tuning (Asumbisa et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Spatial learning was not affected in mice trained and tested in darkness in the current experiments.
source: but here the mice successfully learned to find food and with the same time course of learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 5E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiment data comparing mice trained in darkness versus light.

claim: Heading direction can be derived from optic flow signals.
source: Heading direction can be derived from optic flow signals (Burlingham and Heeger, 2020; Horrocks et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal neurons of rats randomly foraging can develop directional responses based on rich and stable optic flow signals without requiring vestibular input.
source: Hippocampal neurons of rats randomly foraging in a real world or virtual reality environment can develop directional responses based on rich and stable optic flow signals and without requiring vestibular input (Acharya et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Visual input can guide navigation via a central retinal stream for landmarks and a peripheral retinal stream for optic flow input.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that visual input can guide navigation via a central retinal stream for landmarks and a peripheral retinal stream for optic flow input (Saleem, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The vestibular system encodes natural motion.
source: The vestibular system encodes natural motion (Cullen, 2019; Mohammadi et al., 2024)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The vestibular system contributes to the generation of head direction responses.
source: and contributes to the generation of head direction responses (Cullen and Taube, 2017; Taube, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Contextual visual cues of the starting point and arena boundary anchor directional information derived from optic flow, vestibular and proprioceptive signals to fixed environmental features.
source: In agreement with VR studies (Mao et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2024), we hypothesize that contextual visual cues of the starting point and arena boundary anchor directional information derived from optic flow, vestibular and perhaps proprioceptive signals to fixed environmental features.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the current findings and cited VR studies.

claim: Accumulation of path integration error degrades performance as a function of trajectory length in weakly electric fish.
source: and that accumulation of path integration error degrades performance as a function of trajectory length (Mirmiran et al., 2022; Wallach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on electric fish.

claim: It is generally assumed that proximal and/or distal exogenous cues must calibrate the putative path integrator to determine target direction and distance from a start site.
source: Given the presumed accumulation of error by the mammalian path integration mechanism (Etienne et al., 1996), it is generally assumed that proximal and/or distal exogenous cues must calibrate the putative path integrator in order to determine not only target direction but also target distance from a start site (McNaughton et al., 1996; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011; Jayakumar et al., 2019; Etienne and Jeffery, 2004).
evidence: This is a statement of a general assumption in the field, supported by citations.

claim: In the static entrance experiments, the heading direction is constantly updated throughout the entire run.
source: In the static entrance experiments, the heading direction is constantly updated throughout the entire run (Figure 4—figure supplement 3G)
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of heading angle across different trajectory segments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Mice veer toward the food only in the last segment of the trajectory.
source: having the mouse veer toward the food only in the last segment of the trajectory (Figure 4—figure supplement 3Giii).
evidence: This is shown by heading angle data for the 80-85% trajectory segment in Figure 4—figure supplement 3G.

claim: The entropy of the number of hole checks is always lower for near (<20 cm) compared to far (>20 cm) hole checks in static entrance experiments.
source: The entropy of the number of hole checks is always lower for the near compared to far hole checks.
evidence: This is demonstrated by entropy analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Mice are more consistent in choosing the numbers of holes to check when near the food site (<20 cm) versus further from the food (>20 cm).
source: In other words, the mice are more consistent in choosing the numbers of holes to check when near the food site (<20 cm) versus further from the food (>20 cm).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the entropy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The entropy of hole checks decays for both far and near the target conditions consistent with learning food location over trials.
source: The entropy decays for both far and near the target conditions consistent with learning food location over trials, but the decay is twice as steep for the far condition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by entropy analysis over trials shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: During the learning of B, some mice did visit the A location sporadically.
source: During the learning of B, some mice did visit the A location sporadically, making the shaded area larger in panel B.
evidence: This is noted in the description of Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mice did not rely on target A to find B during training of target B.
source: However, they did not rely on target A to find B.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the distance data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B showing mice kept farther from A than expected by chance.

claim: The floor of the maze was washed and rotated 108 times from the first Site A learning trial to the final Probe trial.
source: Our 'wash and rotate the floor' protocol to eliminate odor trails or 'floor scratch cues' results in the floor of the maze being washed and rotated 108 times from the first Site A learning trial to the final Probe trial when Site B and Site A were empty.
evidence: This is stated in the description of Video 1.

claim: The floor rotation results in the same configuration of hole positions relative to every entrance, making the environment identical at every trial for all the mice.
source: The floor rotation results in the same configuration of hole positions relative to every entrance, making the environment identical at every trial for all the mice (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design feature.

claim: C57Bl/6 wild-type male and female mice were used in the experiments.
source: C57Bl/6 wild-type male and female mice were ordered from Charles River, arriving at 8–9 weeks old.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The same results were obtained in both male and female mice and were therefore pooled.
source: Both male and female mice were used; the same results were obtained in both sexes and were therefore pooled.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and data analysis.

claim: All animal procedures were conducted with the approval of the University of Ottawa's Animal Care Committee.
source: All animal procedures were conducted with the approval of the University of Ottawa's Animal Care Committee and in accordance with guidelines set out by the Canadian Council of Animal Care.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The maze floor is washed and rotated between every trial to avoid predictable scratch marks and odor trails.
source: The floor is washed and rotated between every trial to avoid predictable scratch marks and odor trails.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1A caption and Materials and methods.

claim: The distance between each hole is, on average, 10 cm.
source: The distance between each hole is, on average, 10 cm.
evidence: This is a description of the apparatus design.

claim: The illuminance is measured to be 50 lux at the surface of the arena.
source: The illuminance is measured to be 50 lux at the surface of the arena.
evidence: This is a measurement of the experimental conditions.

claim: Dim light was used to allow the mice to properly see all visual cues as well as the maze details.
source: Dim light was used to allow the mice to properly see all visual cues as well as the maze details.
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for the lighting conditions.

claim: This lighting procedure is assumed to not perturb the nocturnal cycle of mice.
source: This procedure is assumed to not perturb the nocturnal cycle of mice (Kronfeld-Schor et al., 2013; Upham and Hafner, 2013).
evidence: This assumption is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Path tracking was done with Ethovision XT15 based on contrast detection.
source: Path tracking was done with Ethovision XT15 (Noldus) based on contrast detection.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection method.

claim: Mice were tracked according to 3 body points at 30 frames per second.
source: Mice were tracked according to 3 body points at 30 frames per second on a 1080 P USB camera with OV2710 CMOS.
evidence: This is a description of the tracking methodology.

claim: The significance cut-off was set at 0.05.
source: The significance cut-off was set at 0.05.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach.
